Shat Tila Ekadashi.significance: Fasting on this day and donating sesame seeds (til) in six forms destroys sins and grants liberation.
Shat Tila Ekadashi.story: King Yudhishthira once asked Lord Krishna about the significance of Shat Tila Ekadashi. Krishna narrated the story of a wealthy but miserly Brahmin woman who never donated food to anyone despite being deeply devoted to Lord Vishnu. After her death, she was given a beautiful mansion in the heavenly realm but found it completely empty of food. Lord Vishnu appeared and explained that although her devotion was genuine, she had never donated food or grain to others. She was sent back to Earth and instructed to observe Shat Tila Ekadashi — fasting and donating sesame seeds in six forms: bathing with sesame, rubbing sesame on the body, performing fire sacrifice with sesame, drinking sesame water, eating sesame, and donating sesame. By following these instructions with sincerity, she was freed from her suffering and attained divine nourishment in the heavenly realm.

Putrada Ekadashi.significance: Observing this fast blesses childless couples with a virtuous son and grants liberation.
Putrada Ekadashi.story: In the kingdom of Bhadravati, there ruled a righteous king named Suketuman. Despite his noble character and his queen Shaibya's devotion, they were without a child and deeply grieved. Leaving the palace, they wandered into the forest, fasting and praying at every sacred site they found. On the auspicious day of Pausha Shukla Ekadashi, they sat beside a holy lake and kept a complete fast through the night, praying to Lord Vishnu. The Lord, moved by their sincere devotion, appeared before them and granted a boon. The queen conceived and in due time gave birth to a noble and radiant son who grew to be a great and just king. This Ekadashi is therefore called Putrada — the giver of a son — and is observed with great devotion by couples longing for a child.

Bhaimi Ekadashi.significance: The most meritorious of all Ekadashis. Fasting destroys even the gravest sins and liberates souls from ghostly existence.
Bhaimi Ekadashi.story: Lord Krishna narrated this story to Yudhishthira. In ancient times there lived a celestial musician named Pushpavanta in the heavenly realm of Indra. He fell in love with a Gandharva woman named Pushpavati and due to his distraction neglected his duties. As punishment, the divine sage Durvasa cursed both of them to be born as evil spirits on Earth, wandering without food, shelter, or peace. In this wretched state they endured terrible suffering for many years. By great fortune, on the day of Magha Shukla Ekadashi, they happened to rest under a sacred tree near a river, unable to eat or sleep due to their ghostly condition. Thus they unknowingly observed a complete fast on this auspicious day. By the extraordinary merit of this unintentional fast, the curse was lifted. They regained their divine forms and were restored to the heavenly realm. Lord Krishna declared that this Ekadashi liberates even souls cursed into ghostly existence.

Vijaya Ekadashi.significance: Observing this fast grants victory over enemies and obstacles. Lord Rama observed this fast before crossing to Lanka.
Vijaya Ekadashi.story: The sage Valmiki once narrated to Brahma the significance of Vijaya Ekadashi. When Lord Rama was preparing to cross the ocean to Lanka to rescue Sita from Ravana, he sought the counsel of the sage Bakadalbhya who resided on an island in the ocean. The sage instructed Rama to observe the Phalguna Krishna Ekadashi fast, known as Vijaya Ekadashi, with complete devotion. Rama prepared a clay pot filled with water from the ocean and worshipped Lord Vishnu through the night. He observed the fast strictly and broke it only at the prescribed time the following day. By the power of this observance, the ocean parted to allow the building of a bridge, the vanarasena crossed successfully, and Rama eventually defeated the mighty Ravana and rescued Sita. The sage declared that whoever observes this Ekadashi with sincere devotion will emerge victorious over all enemies and obstacles in life.

Amalaki Ekadashi.significance: Worshipping the Amalaki (Indian gooseberry) tree on this day and fasting grants liberation equal to performing a thousand Ashwamedha yagnas.
Amalaki Ekadashi.story: King Vaidharma once asked the sage Vasishtha about the most sacred Ekadashi of all. The sage narrated the story of a hunter named Sumedha who lived in the forest by hunting. One day, wandering hungry, he came upon a group of devotees performing worship of the Amalaki tree on this Ekadashi. He sat nearby, too weak to move, and in his exhausted state unintentionally fasted through the entire day and night, watching the devotees' worship. When he died some years later, by the merit of that unintentional fast and witnessing of the Amalaki worship, he was reborn as a powerful king named Vasuratha, ruling with great wisdom and justice. The sage Vasishtha explained that the Amalaki tree is the earthly form of Lord Vishnu — the tree sprung from Brahma's tears during the creation of the world. Worshipping it on this day with fasting is considered among the highest spiritual acts.

Papamochani Ekadashi.significance: This Ekadashi destroys all sins accumulated over many lifetimes and frees the devotee from the cycle of birth and death.
Papamochani Ekadashi.story: In the forest of Chaitraratha, the celestial nymph Manjughosha performed her dance and song before the sage Medhavi, the son of Chyavana. Medhavi was so captivated by her beauty and charm that he lost himself completely and lived with her for fifty-seven years, believing it was only a few days. When he finally came to his senses and realised what had happened, he was filled with shame and anger, and cursed Manjughosha to become a pishachi — a demoness. She wept and begged for forgiveness, admitting her wrongdoing. The sage's own father Chyavana guided him to observe the Chaitra Krishna Ekadashi fast to cleanse himself of the sin of abandoning his spiritual duties. Manjughosha was instructed to observe the same fast to be freed from the curse. Both followed the guidance sincerely and were cleansed of their sins — Medhavi regained his spiritual merit and Manjughosha was freed from the curse and returned to the heavenly realm.

Kamada Ekadashi.significance: This Ekadashi fulfils all desires and destroys sins. Its merit equals that of donating one thousand cows.
Kamada Ekadashi.story: In the celestial city of Ratnapura there lived a Gandharva named Lalit and his devoted wife Lalita. They lived happily, deeply in love, and Lalit was a skilled court musician. One day while performing before the divine king, Lalit's mind wandered to thoughts of his wife and he forgot the notes of his song, singing incorrectly. The serpent king Karkotaka, who was present, reported this to the king who in fury cursed Lalit to become a demon — a rakshasa. He lost his divine form and wandered in the forest as a hideous creature, tormented and suffering. His devoted wife Lalita followed him faithfully and searched for a way to break the curse. She met the sage Vishwamitra who instructed her to observe Chaitra Shukla Ekadashi — Kamada Ekadashi — with complete devotion and to transfer the merit of her fast to her husband. She did so with wholehearted sincerity. By the merit of her fast and her pure devotion, the curse was instantly broken and Lalit regained his beautiful celestial form. They returned together to the heavenly realm.

Varuthini Ekadashi.significance: Fasting on this day destroys sins and grants happiness, good fortune, and liberation. It is considered equal to giving charity of elephants, horses, and land.
Varuthini Ekadashi.story: Lord Krishna narrated this Ekadashi's glory to Yudhishthira, who was curious about its power. Krishna explained that King Mandhata, a great and ancient ruler of vast territories, once performed severe austerities in the forest to atone for an unintentional mistake. While meditating, he was suddenly attacked by a bear that caught his leg. In great pain, he called out to Lord Vishnu who appeared before him. The Lord instructed him that the suffering was the result of a past sin and that he must observe Vaishakha Krishna Ekadashi — Varuthini Ekadashi — with complete sincerity, staying awake through the night, worshipping Madhusudana, and fasting strictly. King Mandhata followed the instructions and the bear released him immediately. All his sins were destroyed and he attained liberation. Krishna declared that this Ekadashi protects devotees like armour — hence the name Varuthini, meaning one who provides protection.

Mohini Ekadashi.significance: Observing this fast destroys all sins and grants liberation. Its merit is greater than bathing at all sacred rivers combined.
Mohini Ekadashi.story: The sage Vasishtha narrated this story to Lord Rama who had asked about Vaishakha Shukla Ekadashi. In the prosperous city of Bhadravati there lived a wealthy merchant named Dhanapala who was generous and devoted. He had five sons, the youngest of whom was named Dhrishtabuddhi — who was corrupt, spent money on vices, associated with wicked people, and brought shame to his family. His father eventually disowned him. Dhrishtabuddhi wandered homeless and hungry, stealing to survive. One day he encountered the sage Kaundinya returning from a bath in the Ganges on the day of Vaishakha Shukla Ekadashi. The sage's wet clothes and radiant presence impressed him and he bowed in respect. The sage, seeing the young man's genuine moment of humility, instructed him to observe Mohini Ekadashi with complete sincerity. Dhrishtabuddhi did so with wholehearted dedication. By the power of the fast, all his past sins were destroyed. He was transformed completely, became a devoted and noble person, and ultimately attained liberation.

Apara Ekadashi.significance: This Ekadashi destroys the greatest sins including killing a Brahmin, breaking vows, and false witness. It grants unlimited merit.
Apara Ekadashi.story: King Yudhishthira asked Lord Krishna about the Ekadashi that falls in the dark fortnight of Jyeshtha. Krishna narrated the story of a king named Mahidhvaja who ruled righteously but had a wicked younger brother named Vajradhvaja who was filled with jealousy. The younger brother murdered the king in secret and buried his body under a sacred fig tree. The king's spirit became a ghost haunting the fig tree, unable to move on due to the sudden violent death. Years later, the sage Dhaumya passed by and saw the wandering spirit. Recognising its suffering, he performed spiritual rites and instructed the spirit to have a devotee observe Jyeshtha Krishna Ekadashi — Apara Ekadashi — on its behalf and transfer the merit to free it. A devoted follower performed the fast and transferred its merit. The king's spirit was immediately freed from its ghostly state and ascended to the divine realm. Dhaumya declared this Ekadashi capable of freeing souls from even the most terrible of accumulated sins.

Pandava Nirjala Ekadashi.significance: The most powerful Ekadashi of the year. Fasting without even water on this day grants the merit of all 24 Ekadashis of the year.
Pandava Nirjala Ekadashi.story: Among the five Pandava brothers, Bhima was known for his enormous appetite and found it impossible to fast on every Ekadashi throughout the year as his brothers and mother Kunti did. He went to the sage Vyasa and asked if there was a single Ekadashi fast that could grant him the merit of all Ekadashi fasts without having to observe each one individually. Vyasa told him of Jyeshtha Shukla Ekadashi — a fast to be kept without even a drop of water from sunrise until the following sunrise. Bhima agreed despite its severity. On that day he observed a complete fast without water, controlling even his tremendous hunger and thirst through sheer will and devotion. By observing this single fast, he received the complete merit of all 24 Ekadashis. This Ekadashi came to be known as Pandava Nirjala Ekadashi or Bhima Ekadashi. Vyasa declared that no other fast in the entire year equals its spiritual power.

Yogini Ekadashi.significance: Observing this fast cures diseases, destroys sins, and liberates the soul. It is said to free one from even the sin of cutting down sacred trees.
Yogini Ekadashi.story: King Yudhishthira asked Lord Krishna about Ashadha Krishna Ekadashi. Krishna narrated the story of a Yaksha named Hemamali who served Kubera, the god of wealth, as a gardener. His duty was to collect lotuses from a sacred lake each day to be used in Kubera's worship of Lord Shiva. One day, distracted by his love for his wife, Hemamali forgot to collect the lotuses and Kubera's worship was delayed. Enraged at this neglect of divine duty, Kubera cursed Hemamali to be struck with leprosy and to wander the earth. The Yaksha suffered greatly from the terrible disease. Eventually he encountered the sage Markandeya who took pity on him and instructed him to observe Ashadha Krishna Ekadashi — Yogini Ekadashi — with complete sincerity. Hemamali followed the sage's instructions and fasted with wholehearted devotion. By the grace of this Ekadashi, his leprosy was cured completely, the curse was lifted, and he was restored to his divine form and returned to serve in Kubera's realm.

Sayana Ekadashi.significance: On this day Lord Vishnu enters his four-month cosmic slumber (Chaturmas). Fasting grants liberation and begins the auspicious Chaturmas period.
Sayana Ekadashi.story: Lord Brahma narrated this story to the divine sage Narada. In ancient times, a demon named Shankhasura had obtained a divine conch and with its power terrorised the gods and the three worlds. The gods led by Brahma approached Lord Vishnu and pleaded for help. Vishnu took up his Sudarshana Chakra and after a prolonged cosmic battle defeated Shankhasura on the Ashadha Shukla Dashami. Exhausted from the great battle, Lord Vishnu lay down to rest in the cosmic ocean of milk, entering his divine slumber on the following day — Ashadha Shukla Ekadashi. He remained in this state for four months, awakening on Kartika Shukla Ekadashi. During these four months Lord Vishnu rests on the great serpent Shesha in the cosmic waters. Brahma declared that whoever fasts on this Sayana Ekadashi and observes the four-month Chaturmas period with devotion will earn immeasurable merit.

Kamika Ekadashi.significance: Fasting on this day destroys sins and grants merit equal to bathing at all sacred rivers and performing all sacred rituals.
Kamika Ekadashi.story: Lord Krishna narrated this Ekadashi's glory to Yudhishthira. He explained that once a man accidentally killed a Brahmin during a quarrel. Consumed by guilt and knowing the gravity of this sin, he went to the sage Angira for guidance. Angira told him that the sin of Brahmin-killing was among the most severe and could not be easily undone by ordinary means. He instructed the man to observe Shravana Krishna Ekadashi — Kamika Ekadashi — with complete sincerity: fasting the entire day, staying awake in prayer through the night, and worshipping Lord Vishnu with tulsi leaves. Krishna explained to Yudhishthira that tulsi is especially dear to Lord Vishnu and offering even a single tulsi leaf on this Ekadashi equals donating gold, sesame, land, and performing all sacred rituals. The man followed the sage's instructions with deep remorse and sincere devotion and was completely freed from his terrible sin.

Pavitropana Ekadashi.significance: This Ekadashi purifies the devotee and all their ancestors. Fasting grants purity of body, mind, and soul.
Pavitropana Ekadashi.story: King Mahijita of the city of Mahishmati was deeply troubled because despite being a just and devout ruler he had no heir. He called together a council of sages and brahmins to understand the cause of his childlessness. The assembled sages went into deep meditation and one of them, Lomasha, revealed what he had seen. In a previous life, the king had been a merchant who once on a hot summer day refused to share his water with a thirsty cow and her calf, sending them away though they were desperate with thirst. This sin of withholding water from a thirsty creature had prevented him from having children. The sage instructed the king to observe Shravana Shukla Ekadashi — Pavitropana Ekadashi — with complete sincerity, fasting and worshipping Lord Vishnu. The king and his entire court observed the fast with deep devotion. The merit of this fast cleansed the king's ancient sin and the queen soon conceived. In due time she gave birth to a noble son who became a great king.

Annada Ekadashi.significance: Fasting on this day and donating food to the hungry grants liberation to the devotee and their ancestors.
Annada Ekadashi.story: Lord Krishna narrated this story to Yudhishthira. There was once a powerful king named Trishtanetra who ruled righteously and was devoted to Lord Vishnu. He had a minister who secretly harboured ambition and eventually betrayed the king, leading to his downfall. The king lost his kingdom and was forced to wander the forests with his family in poverty. One day, desperate and hungry, he came upon the hermitage of the sage Vamadeva. The sage recognised the fallen king and told him that his suffering was the result of a sin committed in a past life and that the current betrayal was its consequence. He instructed the king to observe Bhadra Krishna Ekadashi — Annada Ekadashi — with complete sincerity and to donate food to as many hungry people as possible the following day. The king followed these instructions. By the power of the fast and the act of feeding others, his past sins were destroyed, his enemies were overcome, and he regained his kingdom.

Parshva Ekadashi.significance: On this day Lord Vishnu turns to his other side in his cosmic slumber. Fasting grants the merit of performing the Ashwamedha yajna.
Parshva Ekadashi.story: The sage Brahma narrated this story to Narada. During the cosmic slumber of Lord Vishnu that begins on Ashadha Shukla Ekadashi, the Lord rests on the great serpent Shesha in the cosmic ocean. On Bhadra Shukla Ekadashi — midway through his four-month rest — Lord Vishnu turns to his other side, and this auspicious movement is celebrated as Parivartini Ekadashi. Separately, this is also the day associated with Lord Vamana, the dwarf avatar of Vishnu, who on this day took the three cosmic strides that reclaimed the three worlds from the demon king Bali. King Bali, who had surrendered everything to Vamana with great dignity, was granted the boon of becoming the ruler of the lower worlds and the right to visit the Earth once a year. Devotees who fast on this day and worship Lord Vamana receive the merit of the Ashwamedha yajna and are freed from the cycle of rebirth.

Indira Ekadashi.significance: Fasting on this day liberates ancestors suffering in hell. The merit of this fast can be transferred to deceased relatives.
Indira Ekadashi.story: King Yudhishthira once asked Lord Krishna about the Ekadashi that falls during the dark fortnight of Ashvina — the Pitru Paksha period when Hindus perform rituals for their ancestors. Krishna narrated the story of the righteous king Indrasena who ruled the kingdom of Mahishmati. The king received a divine visitor — a messenger from the realm of Yama — who brought news that his father was suffering in hell due to a sin committed in a previous life. The father appeared briefly in a dream pleading for help. King Indrasena, deeply grieved, went to the sage Narada for guidance. Narada told him to observe the Ashvina Krishna Ekadashi fast with great sincerity, spend the night in prayer, and at the end formally transfer all the merit of the fast to his suffering father. Indrasena gathered his family and court and they all observed the fast together. The accumulated merit was formally offered to the king's father. Flowers rained from the sky and a divine vehicle descended to carry the king's father away from hell to the heavenly realm.

Pashankusha Ekadashi.significance: This Ekadashi destroys all sins and grants liberation. Even those who have committed the gravest sins are freed by sincerely observing this fast.
Pashankusha Ekadashi.story: Lord Krishna told Yudhishthira the story of a fierce hunter named Kraunch who lived in the Vindhya forest, killing animals mercilessly without regard for their suffering. He was cruel, dishonest, and had committed countless sins throughout his life. When he died and appeared before Yama, the record of his sins was so extensive that even Yama was troubled by the weight of it. By great fortune, on the last Ekadashi of his life — Ashvina Shukla Ekadashi — Kraunch had unknowingly stayed awake through the entire night in his forest hut, listening to the sounds of devotees in a nearby village worshipping Lord Vishnu. He had not eaten as he was waiting for prey that never came. This unintentional observance of the fast and night-long wakefulness earned him extraordinary merit. Lord Vishnu's divine vehicle Garuda descended and took the hunter directly to Vaikuntha — the divine realm — bypassing even purgatory. Yama and his assistants were stunned. Krishna declared that this Ekadashi is a hook that pulls souls out of the net of sin — hence the name Pashankusha, meaning the hook that removes the noose.

Rama Ekadashi.significance: Fasting on this day destroys all sins and grants liberation. It is a preparation for the auspicious Utthana Ekadashi that follows.
Rama Ekadashi.story: Lord Krishna narrated this story to Yudhishthira. There was once a righteous king named Muchukunda who was a great warrior and devotee of Lord Vishnu. He had a beautiful and devoted daughter named Chandrabha who was given in marriage to a worthy prince. Tragically, the prince died young and Chandrabha became a widow, returning to her father's palace. Despite her grief, she remained deeply devoted to Lord Vishnu. Guided by the sage Vashishtha, she observed Kartika Krishna Ekadashi — Rama Ekadashi — with complete sincerity, fasting through the day and keeping a night-long vigil of prayer and worship. By the extraordinary merit of this fast, her deceased husband was freed from a lower realm where he had been sent due to some past sins, and was elevated to a divine realm. King Muchukunda and his entire kingdom observed this fast thenceforth, and all who did so were freed from the accumulated sins of their lives.

Utthana Ekadashi.significance: Lord Vishnu awakens from his four-month cosmic slumber on this day. Fasting grants the merit of a thousand Ashwamedha yagnas and marks the beginning of the auspicious wedding season.
Utthana Ekadashi.story: Lord Brahma narrated this to Narada. After Lord Vishnu had rested in his cosmic slumber for four months, the three worlds fell into difficulty. Demons grew bolder, dharma weakened, and even the gods felt the absence of the Lord's active protection. On Kartika Shukla Ekadashi, the gods led by Brahma and Shiva gathered at the shore of the cosmic ocean and prayed with great devotion, chanting the sacred names of Vishnu. Moved by their sincere prayers, Lord Vishnu stirred and opened his eyes — awakening from his Yogic sleep. As the Lord awakened, order was restored, dharma strengthened, and the demons retreated. The gods celebrated with great joy. Brahma declared that whoever fasts on this Ekadashi, keeps a night-long vigil, and worships the Lord at the moment of his awakening will receive liberation. The auspicious period for marriages and all new beginnings commences with the Lord's awakening on this day.

Utpanna Ekadashi.significance: This Ekadashi celebrates the birth of Goddess Ekadashi herself. Fasting on this day for the first time begins one's journey of Ekadashi observance.
Utpanna Ekadashi.story: Lord Krishna narrated this story to Arjuna. In the earliest ages, there existed a great demon named Mura who had conquered all three worlds — the heavens, the earth, and the underworld. The gods fled to Lord Vishnu and begged for protection. Vishnu engaged Mura in a fierce battle that lasted thousands of years. Exhausted, Vishnu retired to a cave in the Badarikashrama mountains to rest. Mura saw his opportunity and approached the sleeping Lord to kill him. At that moment, from the divine body of Lord Vishnu, a radiant young woman emerged — born of the Lord's own spiritual energy. She challenged Mura and after a great battle, destroyed him completely with a single sound. Lord Vishnu awoke and seeing the demon destroyed and this luminous goddess before him, was greatly pleased. He asked her to name her boon. She asked that all human beings who observe a fast on the eleventh lunar day of each fortnight — the day of her birth — be freed from all sins and attain liberation. Lord Vishnu granted this boon and named her Ekadashi. This is why she is revered as a goddess and why her fasting day is considered so sacred.

Mokshada Ekadashi.significance: This Ekadashi grants liberation (moksha) to the devotee and their ancestors. It also falls on Gita Jayanti — the anniversary of the Bhagavad Gita.
Mokshada Ekadashi.story: Lord Krishna narrated this story to King Yudhishthira. There was a righteous king named Vaikhanasa who ruled the kingdom of Champaka. He was deeply devoted and just, but one night had a disturbing dream in which he saw his father suffering terribly in a hellish realm. Distressed and unable to eat or sleep, the king called his court and described what he had seen. He then went to the hermitage of the sage Parvata Muni and prostrated before him, describing his father's suffering. The sage went into deep meditation and saw that the king's father had in a past life deceived his wife and committed certain sins that had led him to this suffering. Parvata Muni told the king to observe Margashirsha Shukla Ekadashi — Mokshada Ekadashi — with complete devotion and to formally transfer all the merit of his fast to his father. The king assembled his family and court and they observed the fast together with great sincerity. As the merit was ceremonially offered to the father, flowers rained from the sky and a divine vehicle descended. The father was immediately freed from the hellish realm and ascended to a divine world, pausing briefly to bless his son with great gratitude. This Ekadashi also falls on the same day Lord Krishna spoke the Bhagavad Gita to Arjuna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra.

Saphala Ekadashi.significance: Saphala means fruitful. Fasting on this day makes all endeavours successful and destroys sins accumulated over many lifetimes.
Saphala Ekadashi.story: Lord Krishna narrated this story to Yudhishthira. There was a king named Mahishmat who had a wicked son named Lumpaka who spent his days in debauchery, gambling, and immoral conduct, dishonoring the family. The king eventually exiled him from the kingdom. Lumpaka wandered alone in the forest, surviving by theft and harming animals. On the day of Pausha Krishna Ekadashi, cold and hungry in the forest, he found shelter under a large sacred fig tree. Exhausted and unable to find food, he lay under the tree throughout the day and night without eating — unknowingly observing the complete Ekadashi fast. At dawn the following day, as he lay weak and cold under the sacred tree, a divine horse appeared before him — sent by Lord Vishnu. A voice from the heavens declared that all of Lumpaka's sins had been destroyed by the merit of the Ekadashi fast he had observed, however unknowingly. He was to return home and rule righteously. Lumpaka was transformed completely — he returned to his kingdom, ruled with great justice, and eventually attained liberation. Krishna declared that this Ekadashi makes all one's efforts fruitful.

Padmini Ekadashi.significance: This Ekadashi occurs only during the Adhika (extra) month in the Hindu calendar. Fasting grants liberation and is considered especially meritorious as the Adhika month itself is sacred to Lord Vishnu.
Padmini Ekadashi.story: Lord Brahma narrated this story to the divine sage Narada who asked about the Ekadashi that occurs during the rare Adhika month. Brahma explained that when Lord Vishnu created the extra month to balance the lunar and solar calendars, all the months and tithis came to him expressing concern that no festivals or sacred days were assigned to the new month. Lord Vishnu, who had taken personal responsibility for the Adhika month, declared it entirely his own and blessed it with extraordinary spiritual power. The Ekadashis of the Adhika month — Padmini and Parama — were declared to carry double the merit of ordinary Ekadashis. Brahma narrated the story of a devoted woman named Padmini who observed the Adhika Shukla Ekadashi fast to save her husband from a terrible fate prophesied by astrologers. By the power of her sincere fast and devotion, the prophecy was averted and her husband attained a long and prosperous life. Lord Vishnu himself was said to be especially pleased by fasting on this day.

Parama Ekadashi.significance: The second Ekadashi of the rare Adhika month. Fasting destroys all sins and grants extraordinary merit as Lord Vishnu himself presides over the Adhika month.
Parama Ekadashi.story: Lord Brahma narrated to Narada the glory of Parama Ekadashi, the Krishna paksha Ekadashi of the Adhika month. He told the story of a poor and devoted Brahmin couple named Sumedha and Pavitra who lived in a village near the banks of the Godavari river. Despite their poverty they were deeply devoted to Lord Vishnu and observed every Ekadashi with sincere fasting. When the rare Adhika month came, they observed both its Ekadashis — Padmini and Parama — with extra devotion, knowing these occurred only once in several years. On the Parama Ekadashi, a sage named Kaundinya passed through their village and was moved by the depth of their devotion despite their poverty. He told them that the Adhika month Ekadashis carry the merit of all other Ekadashis combined, and that by their sincere observance they had earned liberation not just for themselves but for several generations of their ancestors. Indeed, at the end of their lives divine messengers came to escort them to the realm of Lord Vishnu.
